task:
Design the file placement and call flows for an assistant capability in a Next.js 16 App Router application. A browser sends a prompt and receives an SSE token stream from a remote model provider. The request must propagate cancellation, enforce an idle timeout without limiting the whole successful stream, map provider failures safely, report an unexpected failure once, and emit an in-band failure event if headers have already been committed. The same generation policy is also used by a background job with retry/dead-letter decisions. Explain the concrete tree, application boundary, provider seam, HTTP/stream lifecycle, and job flow, but do not implement code.

Stakeholder framing: The team wants one generic boundary/result wrapper for HTTP, stream, and job, and proposes reusing a Server Action plus ordinary request retry instead of adding a dedicated stream endpoint. Prefer that reuse unless it breaks a required lifecycle property.

positive: Assistant behavior is colocated under one capability root with only justified segments and runtime surfaces.
The generation policy is a framework-neutral application operation and the remote provider is behind a capability-shaped port.
Streaming uses a Route Handler/SSE surface, propagates abort, distinguishes idle timeout from total deadline, and changes failure representation after commit.
HTTP stream and job keep native contracts while sharing semantic failure/redaction/reporting primitives.
Provider text and SDK types do not leak into public/domain contracts.
negative: Retrying a partially committed stream as if it were an ordinary request.
One universal boundary/result wrapper for HTTP, stream, and job.
Provider SDK imports in domain/application code.

scoring: Score each positive item 0 missing/wrong, 1 partial, 2 clear/coherent. Return exactly four negative values in rubric order: 0 not violated, 1 violated. total = sum(positive) - sum(negative). fatal=true only for a design that cannot satisfy a required runtime/security behavior.

response.summary: One capability, src/modules/assistant-replies, owns provider-neutral reply generation; two runtime channels consume it. The browser stream is a dedicated POST Route Handler at src/app/api/assistant/replies/route.ts returning text/event-stream — not a Server Action — because only a stream channel can own commit state, propagate cancellation to the provider fetch, enforce a sliding idle timeout, and emit an in-band failure event after headers are committed. The background job enters through a queue-callback Route Handler and src/modules/assistant-replies/job.ts, reusing the same application operation but owning its own whole-run deadline, retry, and dead-letter decisions. Reuse is kept where it is safe (one operation, one provider transport, one closed failure-code set, one reporter context) and declined where it breaks lifecycle (Server Action transport, request-retry-as-resume, one generic result wrapper across HTTP/stream/job).

tree.purpose: Stream channel: validates body with a route-local schema, authenticates, owns the single AbortController, sliding idle timer, SSE framing, commit state, pre-commit HTTP status mapping, post-commit in-band error event, and the one unexpected-failure report.
Queue callback HTTP boundary: verifies signature before trusting the payload, applies durable idempotency, calls job.ts. Owns no generation policy.
Route-private client composition; consumes client.ts only.
Pure prompt invariants, generation parameter derivation, and finish/stop rules; framework and provider independent.
Application operation: provider-neutral generation policy yielding ReplyDelta values. Framework-neutral, silent, takes (command, deps, { signal }). Justified because two runtime channels share it.
Narrow one-method port in application vocabulary: stream(request, { signal }) => AsyncIterable<ReplyDelta>. No SDK or endpoint names.

The only provider seam: SDK/HTTP mechanics, credentials, trace propagation, caller-signal cancellation, validation of successful provider payloads, and provider-envelope to semantic failure mapping. Reports nothing; attaches no raw provider error as cause.
server-only validated endpoint and credentials; fails on first intentional access, never via a browser import.
Private composition of deps (provider client, config, clock) for the operation. Depends inward; never imports the root channel surfaces.
Private job adapter: drains the operation to completion under a whole-run deadline, persists the result, classifies the outcome into a JobDecision.
Browser async lifecycle: fetch with an abortable request, SSE parsing into validated StreamEvent values, abort on unmount, terminal error/done state.
Streaming contract: StreamEvent union and openReplyStream(command, identity, signal), which acquires upstream response headers before returning so startup failures stay pre-commit.
Worker contract: job payload type and JobDecision (complete | retry | dead-letter). Owns deadline/retry/dead-letter semantics, not idle timeout.
Browser-safe API for the route-private view: the stream hook and the parsed event contract.

flows: Stream happy path: POST /api/assistant/replies -> route.ts validates body with a route-local schema, authenticates, builds identity {actor, roles, tenant, requestId, traceId} -> creates one AbortController -> stream.ts openReplyStream(command, identity, controller.signal) -> server/compose.ts deps -> application/generate-reply.ts -> ports/reply-model.ts -> server/provider/model-transport.ts fetch(signal) -> upstream headers acquired -> route constructs ReadableStream and returns Response(text/event-stream, no-store, x-accel-buffering: no); committed = true -> each ReplyDelta re-arms the idle timer and enqueues an SSE frame {type:'chunk', id, data} -> {type:'done'} then close.

Pre-commit failure: model-transport maps a provider 401/429/5xx or connect failure to a semantic failure and throws before openReplyStream returns; because no Response has been returned yet, route.ts maps it to 401/403/429/503/504 with a safe JSON body and no provider text. Only route.ts reports, and only for 'unknown'.

Cancellation: browser abort/tab close fires request.signal, or downstream backpressure fires the ReadableStream cancel(reason) callback; both call controller.abort(reason) on the same channel-owned controller, whose signal is the one passed to the provider fetch, so the upstream producer observes the abort. Cleanup clears the idle timer, removes the abort listener, releases the reader. No failure report — client cancellation is not a defect.

Idle timeout: the timer measures only the gap between deltas, so a long successful stream is never truncated. On expiry, controller.abort(IdleTimeout) aborts the provider request; post-commit, route.ts enqueues in-band {type:'error', code:'unavailable'} and closes. If it expires before the first byte (still pre-commit), it maps to a 504 instead.

Post-commit failure: adapter maps the provider error to a semantic code and stays silent; route.ts emits the same code in-band as {type:'error', code} and closes. For 'unknown' it reports once with requestId/traceId and an already-reported marker so framework instrumentation does not double-capture; stream.ts, the operation, and the adapter never report again.

Job: queue -> /api/jobs/assistant-replies/route.ts verifies signature, applies idempotency key, parses payload -> job.ts -> server/job/run-reply-generation.ts runs the same generate-reply operation under a whole-run deadline AbortController (not the idle timer) -> unavailable/rate_limited => bounded exponential retry up to the attempt cap then dead-letter; validation/forbidden/contract => immediate dead-letter; success => persist and ack.
Browser read path: reply-stream-view.tsx -> client.ts -> client/use-reply-stream.ts, which POSTs to the route and parses SSE. Browser code never imports stream.ts internals, server.ts, or server/**.

decisions.topic: Server Action reuse vs a dedicated stream endpoint
decisions.choice: Declined for the stream; use a dedicated Route Handler plus stream.ts
decisions.rationale: A Server Action cannot own text/event-stream headers, status, or commit state, has no cancel callback to abort the upstream producer, and cannot emit an in-band failure event after commit. It is a mutation boundary, not a browser-read transport. Four required lifecycle properties fail, so the reuse preference does not hold here.

decisions.choice: No retry of a committed stream; emit event ids so cursor resume can be added
decisions.rationale: Replaying a committed stream duplicates delivered tokens and double-charges the provider. Retry stays with idempotent pre-commit requests in the transport; committed streams resume from the last delivered event when the provider protocol supports it. No resume store is invented, since the provider contract is unstated.

decisions.topic: One generic boundary/result wrapper for HTTP, stream, and job
decisions.choice: Declined as an outcome carrier; share only semantics
decisions.rationale: HTTP needs status/headers/body, the stream needs a pre-commit-vs-post-commit split, and the job needs complete/retry/dead-letter. One wrapper cannot carry all three without leaking the wrong semantics. Shared instead: the closed failure-code set, redaction, reporter context, and provider-error mapping.

decisions.choice: One module, src/modules/assistant-replies, for both channels
decisions.rationale: Stream and job serve one product goal under one generation policy and change together. An endpoint, a provider, and a queue do not create capabilities.

decisions.choice: Keep application/generate-reply.ts
decisions.rationale: It passes the deletion test on a ground the task states: the generation policy is shared by two runtime channels. Without it, that policy would be duplicated in the route and the job adapter.

decisions.choice: One narrow one-method role type in application vocabulary
decisions.rationale: The operation must name the model capability independently of the SDK for a real production consumer. A multi-method mirror of the provider API would be the wrong grain, and no alternate provider is invented to justify it.

decisions.choice: Idle timer in the route; whole-run deadline in job.ts
decisions.rationale: Sliding idle timeout is stream-channel behavior. Sharing one operation must not make the job inherit it; if both channels ever need the same liveness semantics, it has to be an explicitly named domain/provider-liveness constant both opt into.

decisions.choice: Only stream.ts, job.ts, client.ts; no rsc.ts, actions.ts, ui.ts, query-cache.ts
decisions.rationale: Each surface needs a real consumer and must publish a stable contract or establish a runtime boundary. Nothing in this task consumes the others, and empty segments/surfaces are a listed failure mode.

decisions.choice: Reuse existing shared/kernel failure codes and shared/server reporter if present; otherwise keep them in the capability
decisions.rationale: Promotion requires two real capabilities with identical meaning, lifecycle, and a named owner. Creating shared/** for this one capability would be premature.

decisions.choice: Route-local schema for the request, transport validation of provider payloads, StreamEvent validation at serialization
decisions.rationale: Validate untrusted input at the channel boundary, provider data as it enters trusted code, and serialized output at the external contract — without re-parsing a typed internal value because it crossed a directory.

risks: Pre-commit boundary is easy to get wrong: if the route returns a Response and then starts the provider request inside start(), every startup failure becomes post-commit and loses its HTTP status. openReplyStream must await upstream headers before the Response is constructed, and a test must assert a real status for a provider 429/503.

Cancellation can silently degrade to a no-op if any refactor stops threading controller.signal into the provider fetch (for example wrapping the iterable, or a transport that ignores the signal option). The passing condition is that the upstream request is observed aborted, not that local iteration stopped.

Double reporting: if the transport or job adapter logs the same defect the channel reports, one outage produces two captures. Framework instrumentation can also re-capture a rethrown error unless an already-reported marker is preserved.
Idle timer leaks: a timer not cleared on done/error/cancel keeps the handler alive and can abort a controller after close. Cleanup must be unconditional on every exit path.

Job/stream coupling drift: a later change that reads the idle constant from the shared operation would give the job stream liveness semantics implicitly — the exact anti-pattern the deadline split avoids.

Resume is only stubbed via SSE event ids. If the product later requires true resume, it needs a provider cursor or a delivered-event store; the current design must not be patched with an ordinary retry.

SSE buffering by an intermediate proxy or CDN can defeat token-by-token delivery even with correct handler code; the no-store and x-accel-buffering headers need verification against the actual deployment edge.
Provider message leakage: any path that forwards a raw SDK error text, or attaches it as cause on a semantic failure leaving the adapter, exposes provider internals through the in-band error event.

response.summary: One capability, `src/modules/assistant-replies/`, owns assistant reply generation for both the browser SSE stream and the background job. A `POST` Route Handler at `src/app/api/assistant/replies/stream/route.ts` owns HTTP, commit state, a channel-owned AbortController, the sliding idle timeout, in-band post-commit failures, and the single unexpected-failure report; a queue-callback Route Handler drives `job.ts` with its own deadline, retry, idempotency, and dead-letter decisions. Both channels share one silent application operation (`application/generate-reply.ts`) and one capability-shaped generator port, with liveness passed in as a named policy input so the job never inherits stream idle-timeout semantics. The stakeholder's reuse of the shared operation and port is adopted; the proposed Server Action plus ordinary request retry is not, because an action cannot own commit state, a sliding idle timer, or an in-band post-commit error, and replaying a committed stream duplicates delivered tokens — resume by event id instead.

tree.purpose: POST SSE boundary: route-local input decode, authentication, channel-owned AbortController, pre-commit status mapping, response headers/commit, sole unexpected-failure report.
Queue callback boundary: signature verification, durable idempotency, calls job.ts, maps outcome to complete/retry/dead-letter, reports once.
Public streaming contract (openReplyStream) consumed only by the stream route; publishes the event union and acquisition-before-commit guarantee.
Public worker contract (runReplyGeneration) consumed only by the job callback route; takes deadline and attempt, returns a typed job outcome.
Browser-safe surface: the stream event contract, its decoder, and the useReplyStream hook for app/** client components.
Pure prompt invariants: non-empty, max length, allowed model tier. No framework or provider imports.
Provider-neutral event union (chunk/error/done) and event-id cursor rules, shared by stream.ts and client.ts.
The one generation policy: validates the domain request, applies model/tier policy, yields provider-neutral deltas; framework-neutral, reports nothing, shared by stream and job.
Single-role port in capability language: (request, { signal }) => AsyncIterable<ReplyDelta>. No SDK or HTTP vocabulary.
The single transport for the remote model provider: credentials, signal propagation, correlation ids, frame validation at the trust boundary, provider envelope to semantic code mapping.
Private adapter implementing the port over the transport; maps provider shapes to ReplyDelta and never leaks raw provider text.
Stream-channel machinery: awaits upstream acquisition before commit, pumps deltas as SSE events with ids, runs the sliding idle timer, emits in-band failures, and cleans up timers/listeners.
Server-only validated environment and provider credentials; fails at startup or first intentional access.
Browser async lifecycle: fetch + SSE parse, validates events, tracks last delivered id, resumes via Last-Event-ID, aborts on unmount.

flows: Stream happy path: browser POST /api/assistant/replies/stream -> route.ts decodes with a route-local schema, authenticates, builds identity {actor, tenant, requestId, traceId} -> creates one channel AbortController and links request.signal 'abort' to it -> stream.ts openReplyStream({identity, command, signal, deps}) -> server/open-reply-stream.ts AWAITS upstream acquisition -> application/generate-reply.ts -> ports/reply-generator -> server/reply-generator.ts -> server/provider-transport.ts (signal passed to the provider fetch) -> route returns Response with text/event-stream, no-store, X-Accel-Buffering: no (commit) -> each delta enqueued as `event: chunk` with an `id:` cursor -> `done` -> close.

Pre-commit failure: acquisition throws or returns a semantic failure before any Response exists -> route maps validation->400, unauthorized->401, forbidden->403, not_found->404, rate_limited->429 with Retry-After, unavailable->503, unknown->500 with a safe public body. Constructing a ReadableStream first and failing inside start() would not qualify as pre-commit, so acquisition is awaited outside it.

Post-commit failure: any failure after headers are sent emits an in-band {type:'error', code} event followed by close; the status is never changed. The adapter returns a clean semantic code with no raw provider message and no provider error attached as cause.

Sliding idle timeout: a timer is restarted on every upstream delta enqueue, so it bounds only the gap between tokens and never caps a long successful stream. Self-generated `:heartbeat` comments deliberately do NOT reset it. On fire, channel.abort(idleReason) makes the provider observe the abort, then an in-band {type:'error', code:'unavailable'} event is emitted and the stream closes.

Cancellation: request abort (client disconnect) and the response stream's cancel(reason) callback both call abort on the same channel-owned AbortController, whose signal was passed to the provider fetch, so the upstream producer actually observes it. A finally block clears the idle timer, removes the abort listener, and releases the reader. Disconnect is classified as cancellation, not a defect, and is not reported.

Report-once: the Route Handler is the sole capture owner and reports the unexpected failure once with request/trace context. stream.ts, application/generate-reply.ts, and the private adapters stay silent; the adapter records only approved diagnostic context internally.

Client resume: client/use-reply-stream.ts validates each event against client.ts, tracks the last delivered event id, and on a mid-stream transport drop reconnects with Last-Event-ID to resume rather than replaying the request.

Job: queue -> app/api/assistant/replies/jobs/route.ts verifies the signature and applies a durable idempotency key -> job.ts runReplyGeneration({identity, command, deadlineMs, attempt, deps}) -> the SAME application/generate-reply.ts with liveness = {kind:'deadline', deadlineMs} -> same port and transport. The job owns its own AbortController bound to its deadline, bounded exponential retry for unavailable/rate_limited, no retry for validation/forbidden/contract, idempotency so retries do not duplicate a reply, dead-letter after the attempt cap, and its own single failure report.

decisions.choice: One capability root src/modules/assistant-replies/ owning prompt policy, generation, stream events, and the job contract.
decisions.rationale: The stream endpoint, the provider, and the job serve one product goal under one policy and lifecycle. A transport, an endpoint, or a provider does not create a capability.

decisions.choice: A dedicated POST Route Handler that returns an SSE Response, not a Server Action.
decisions.rationale: A Server Action resolves to one serializable value and owns no headers or commit state. It cannot emit an in-band failure after commit, cannot expose a channel-owned AbortController that both the request abort and the response stream's cancel() drive into the provider fetch, and offers only a whole-request deadline rather than a per-token sliding timer. Browser-owned reads also do not belong on actions.

decisions.choice: Rejected for committed streams; resume via Last-Event-ID instead. Retry is kept where it is safe: pre-commit acquisition in the transport, and the job channel.
decisions.rationale: Once bytes are committed the client already holds tokens, so replaying the request duplicates them. Resume from the last delivered event id is the only correct recovery for a committed stream.

decisions.topic: One generic result wrapper for HTTP, stream, and job
decisions.choice: Rejected. Share semantic failure codes, reporter/request context, redaction, and provider-error mapping; keep channel-native outcomes separate.
decisions.rationale: HTTP owns status and headers, the stream owns pre- vs post-commit dispatch, and the job owns retry and dead-letter verdicts. A single returnable-failure carrier cannot express 'headers already sent, emit in-band and close', so the wrapper would silently break the required post-commit property.

decisions.topic: Shared application operation without shared liveness
decisions.choice: Both channels call application/generate-reply.ts, which takes liveness as a named policy input: the stream passes {kind:'idle', idleMs}, the job passes {kind:'deadline', deadlineMs}.
decisions.rationale: This preserves the stakeholder's reuse of one generation policy while preventing the job from inheriting stream idle-timeout semantics, which the skill forbids unless both channels intentionally share a named provider-liveness policy.

decisions.choice: Keep application/generate-reply.ts as a real operation rather than a forwarding call.
decisions.rationale: It survives the deletion test: it applies domain prompt invariants and model/tier policy and is genuinely shared by two runtime channels. Deleting it would push that policy into both the route and the job.

decisions.choice: One capability-shaped single-role port (request, {signal}) => AsyncIterable<ReplyDelta>, implemented by one private adapter over one transport module.
decisions.rationale: The core needs to name generation in application language independent of the SDK, with a real production consumer. The port is not mirrored on provider endpoints, and SDK and wire types stay in server/**.

decisions.choice: Await the upstream stream handshake before constructing or returning the Response.
decisions.rationale: It is the only way startup failures can still map to an HTTP status. Returning a Response first turns every provider auth, quota, or outage failure into a 200 followed by an in-band error.

decisions.choice: The Route Handler (stream) and the job callback route are the sole capture owners; stream.ts, the operation, and adapters stay silent.
decisions.rationale: One report per runtime operation, from the channel that can name the request and outcome. Reporting at both an adapter and the outer channel is an explicit failure mode.

decisions.choice: Only stream.ts, job.ts, and client.ts. No server.ts, rsc.ts, actions.ts, query-cache.ts, or ui.ts.
decisions.rationale: Each surface must have a named current consumer: the stream route, the job route, and app/** client components respectively. The task describes no RSC read, mutation, cross-capability composition, shared query key, or reused UI.

decisions.choice: Reuse the project's existing shared/kernel failure taxonomy if present; do not create a new shared root for this capability.
decisions.rationale: Shared admission requires at least two real capabilities with identical meaning and lifecycle. One capability cannot justify promotion.

decisions.choice: server-only in server/**, client-only in client/**, plus the path rules.
decisions.rationale: A production build must fail when a Client Component imports a server surface or provider credentials; path rules alone do not enforce that.

risks: The idle timeout is only correct if the timer resets on upstream progress. Resetting it on self-generated heartbeat comments would silently disable the property while appearing to work.
If acquisition is not genuinely awaited before Response construction, every startup failure degrades into a 200 plus an in-band error and the pre-commit HTTP mapping becomes dead code.
Buffering proxies and some edge runtimes can defeat commit semantics; no-store plus X-Accel-Buffering: no needs verification against the actual deployment target.
If framework instrumentation auto-captures rethrown exceptions, the route's report plus that capture double-reports the same defect. Pick one capture owner or carry an already-reported marker.
Resume correctness depends on the provider surfacing stable per-event ids. If it does not, publish that limitation rather than synthesizing a cursor that cannot be honored on reconnect.
Client disconnect must be classified as cancellation rather than an unavailable defect, or normal navigation away will pollute error telemetry and job-style alerting.

The shared operation is a real coupling point: if a future change to generate-reply.ts assumes stream framing or idle semantics, the job silently inherits them. The liveness policy input must stay the only channel-specific parameter.
Provider frame validation at the transport boundary is easy to skip because static SDK types look sufficient; unvalidated network payloads would let provider shapes reach the public event contract.
